title: An FP16 row normalized in FP32, including the reduction's return path
surface: ub_to_reg_unpack and reg_to_ub_downsample around FP32 work on an FP16 register's even lanes; cast with RegLayout.ZERO both ways; cadd then reg_to_ub_single / ub_to_reg_single to broadcast lane 0; sqrt and div standing in for a missing rsqrt; muls / adds / mul / dup
study_for: The reduction's return path, which no other example here walks. `cadd` leaves the whole-register sum in lane 0 and nothing else; `reg_to_ub_single` parks that one lane in a UB cell and `ub_to_reg_single` brings it back across all 64. That round trip through memory is the mechanism -- there is no register-to-register broadcast of a single lane in this vocabulary, and a kernel that assumed one would be reading lane 0's value in lane 0 only.

FP16 data, FP32 arithmetic, and the even lanes are the seam between them. `ub_to_reg_unpack` puts 64 dense FP16 elements on the even lanes of an FP16 register; `cast` with `RegLayout.ZERO` widens exactly those into a 64-lane FP32 register; the result narrows back onto the even lanes and `reg_to_ub_downsample` compacts them. The cast policy in docs/api/formats.md owns why the layout selects those lanes and why the mask width matters.

No `rsqrt` exists here, so the scale is `sqrt` then `div` with a register of ones. That is two instructions and one extra rounding compared with a fused reciprocal square root -- and the comparison is still bitwise, which is the useful part: the reference mirrors the same operation order in FP64.

`eps` is observable in exactly one case, and the case matrix is built around that. `zero_row` sends an all-zero row through: with the bias it normalizes to a finite zero, without it the row divides by zero and arrives NaN. Everywhere else 2^-10 is far below one FP16 ulp of the result, so a matrix without that row cannot distinguish an implementation that applies eps from one that drops it.

Why bitwise rather than a tolerance. The kernel computes in FP32 and narrows once with ties-to-even; the reference computes in FP64 and narrows once. On these four cases they agree in every bit, so a one-ulp disagreement is a finding rather than noise -- and the failure output prints the ulp distance for exactly that reason.
do_not_copy_when: You were going to drop the epsilon because it never shows up. It shows up on an all-zero row, and an all-zero row is not exotic in a normalization -- a masked-out block produces one.

You expect bitwise agreement to survive a different case matrix. It holds for these inputs and this operation order. Widen the domain, reorder the reduction, or fuse the reciprocal square root, and the right answer is a stated tolerance, not this comparison.

You need more than one participant. This is `block_dim=1` and one vector participant owns every row. Splitting rows across cores is straightforward, but the reduction's UB cell is then per-core state and nothing here establishes that.

Your reduction is not over a whole register. `cadd` reduces all 64 lanes; a row shorter than the register needs a mask, and then lane 0 holds the sum of the lanes the mask admitted -- which is a different kernel with a different reference.
